title: Bhagat Singh Thind, 1923
hook: a Sikh army veteran is denied US citizenship by the Supreme Court

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Komagata Maru: two months in Vancouver harbor, and your line, they were turned away. Did you welcome a newcomer? Today, a man who got in, served, and was still told he didn't belong. Day three hundred seventeen.

There's an old photograph of a young man in a United States Army uniform from the First World War. Stiff collar, straight back, and on his head, a turban. His name is Bhagat Singh Thind. He came from Punjab to study, worked in lumber mills in Oregon to pay for college, and when America went to war, he enlisted. He served. He was honorably discharged. Then he applied to become a citizen of the country he'd served. His case went all the way to the Supreme Court. Today: Bhagat Singh Thind.
screen: `A TURBAN AND AN ARMY UNIFORM.` → `MILLS, COLLEGE, THE WAR.` → `ALL THE WAY TO THE SUPREME COURT.`

segments.voice: At the time, American law allowed only certain people to become citizens by naturalization, and the key words were white persons. Thind was granted citizenship after the war, and the government fought it. His lawyers argued that, by the science of the day, people from north India were counted in the same broad family as Europeans. In February 1923, the Supreme Court ruled against him, all nine justices. They said that whatever the scientists said, in the common understanding of ordinary people he was not white, and so could not be a citizen. The ruling hit hard. Other Indian Americans had their citizenship taken away. Some lost land they had bought, because non-citizens couldn't own it in California. Families who had built lives were told, in effect, you're guests here, not members. And here's what Thind did next. He stayed. He kept teaching and writing, lecturing across America about the spiritual teachings of the Gurus and about finding the divine within. And in 1936, a new law gave citizenship to veterans of the First World War, and he finally became a citizen, in New York. It took ten more years before Indians in general could become American citizens. Now, his name. Bhagat means a devotee. Singh, lion, the name every Sikh man carries since the Khalsa. A devoted lion. He was patient, and he was stubborn in the good way. The court said he didn't belong. His life said otherwise. He belonged.
screen: `CITIZENSHIP FOR WHITE PERSONS ONLY.` · `FEBRUARY 1923: NINE AGAINST HIM.` · `HE STAYED, AND TAUGHT.` · `1936: CITIZEN AT LAST.` · then, large: `HE BELONGED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand up for someone's belonging. Settle, and breathe. Think of a moment, maybe recent, when someone was made to feel they didn't belong: at school, at work, online, in your family. Maybe it was you. Picture it clearly, but gently. Now picture a different ending, where someone quietly says, they're with us. What would it take for that someone to be you, next time? Find one sentence you could say. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bhagat Singh Thind. A Sikh veteran of the First World War denied citizenship by the Supreme Court in 1923, who stayed, taught, and became a citizen in 1936.
Your line: he belonged. Today, if you see someone left at the edge of a group, say or do one small thing that tells them they belong. Day three hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Sikh Americans remember Bhagat Singh Thind as a veteran and teacher, and his case is often taught in American history and civil-rights classes.

fork.setup: you're Bhagat Singh Thind in 1923. the highest court in the land has just said you can't be a citizen. what do you do?

stop wearing the turban to fit in.

original.note: Gurmukhi: singh, lion; the name every Sikh man carries since the Khalsa of 1699.

trapdoor: what you thought: serving your country made you a citizen.
what it means: a Sikh veteran was told he could not belong, and stayed until the law caught up with him.
what a scholar hears: United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind (1923) turned on the words 'white persons'; the Luce–Celler Act of 1946 opened naturalization to Indians.

notes: The 1918 citizenship grant (Washington, revoked days later), the 1920 Oregon grant, and the 1936 New York naturalization are compressed to 'granted after the war' and '1936'; confirm.
The decision was unanimous (opinion by Justice Sutherland); confirm.
The claim that the old photograph shows him in a turban in US Army uniform is widely reproduced; confirm.
The phrase 'white persons' is quoted as the statute's language inside the trapdoor and teach; it is a legal term, not a quotation from a scripture.
